justification: Reads well ahead of the best-ranking pages for "tcp vs udp" on almost every axis a design critic controls: reading rhythm alternates prose / runnable C# / real measured output / diagram cleanly, heading hierarchy is correct and varied (no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion), all three figures are legible and theme-correct at both desktop and 390px-mobile width in both light and dark (checked every part of desktop-light and mobile-dark, plus fold+2 of desktop-dark and mobile-light), code blocks keep their operative content within the visible ~40-column window with no clipped point-of-the-example, callouts and the four exercises are used correctly (solutions collapsed, not given away above the fold), and the sources list is complete and well-formatted. Lighthouse is 98/100/100/100, zero console errors, zero broken links, zero page-level horizontal overflow (mobileOverflowPx: 0). Wikipedia's TCP and UDP pages, by contrast, have no runnable code, no real measurements, and only static header/handshake diagrams, so on depth and illustration this article is clearly ahead of them, consistent with a 10 on that axis alone. What holds the overall score well below the 8.5 ("MDN/Real Python, nits only") anchor is that the article's two comparison tables -- the exact device the query "tcp vs udp" is asking for -- lose an entire column off-screen by default at phone width, confirmed identically in both mobile-dark and mobile-light screenshots. That is more than a nit for the site's majority mobile audience on a compare-shape article, so this lands at 7.5: clearly better illustrated and more rigorous than the best-ranking pages, but with a real, repeated mobile readability defect in its central content device.

issues.location: "What each one actually promises" table (Guarantee/TCP/UDP) and "What the guarantees cost in bytes" table (blank/UDP/TCP), both confirmed on mobile-dark-part02/part13 and mobile-light-part02
issues.problem: At 390px width, each table shows only about 2 of its 3 columns before the fade; the reader has to notice and perform a horizontal scroll to see the rest. In the first table the entire UDP column is off-screen on load (only Guarantee + TCP are visible); in the second table the entire TCP column is off-screen (only the blank label column + UDP are visible). For an article whose whole point is TCP vs UDP, hiding one full side of the comparison by default is a real readability defect, not a cosmetic one. The root cause matches the exact failure mode docs/WRITER_GUIDE.md section 7 warns about: cells are full sentences ("Retransmits until acknowledged or the connection gives up", "4-way FIN exchange, then TIME-WAIT (RFC 9293, section 3.6)") rather than the short phrases the guide calls for, so a nominally-3-column table still overflows.
issues.fixLooksLike: Rewrite every cell in both tables as a short phrase rather than a sentence (e.g. "Retransmits until acked" / "Lost datagram is just gone", "4-way FIN, then TIME-WAIT"), so each column comfortably fits within roughly 40 characters at phone width and no column is hidden without a deliberate scroll. If phrase-length cells still do not fit three across, restructure the guarantees table as two stacked two-column tables (TCP | UDP each on their own) or a definition list instead, per the guide's own fallback advice.

issues.location: Both comparison tables, site-wide table rendering (lighthouse.json failing audits)
issues.problem: Lighthouse's `td-has-header` audit scores 0: the tables' data cells (e.g. the "Delivery", "Header" row-label cells) are not associated with a header via `scope="row"` or `headers`/`id`, so a screen reader traversing a cell cannot always announce which row it is in. This does not currently pull down the Accessibility category score (still 100 in this run) but is a genuine, repeated gap on every article that uses a comparison table.
issues.fixLooksLike: Have the shared Markdown-table renderer add `scope="row"` to the first `<td>` in each row (or `scope="col"` plus row `id`s if a different scheme is preferred). This is not something a GFM table in an article's Markdown can express, so it belongs in the shell/table component, not per-article.
